turns.text: Daylight saving time disrupts sleep, harms health, and saves little energy. Studies link the spring transition to more heart attacks, strokes, and workplace injuries. Farmers, parents, and shift workers struggle with confused schedules. Modern lighting and appliances have erased any meaningful electricity savings, while airlines and computers still lose money fixing clock errors twice a year. People deserve stable mornings that match natural light and biological rhythms. Abolishing daylight saving time would end the confusion, protect public health, and let communities keep one consistent, sensible schedule all year long.

The motion ignores the real cost of permanent standard time. The 2007 U.S. extension of daylight saving time cut national electricity use by about 0.5 percent, and a 2017 meta-analysis found small but real savings. More importantly, longer evenings reduce crime; one study found robbery falls about 7 percent when clocks move forward. Evening light also boosts retail activity and exercise. Changing the whole year to standard time would mean dark winter afternoons, hurting commuters, children, and small businesses. The better reform is permanent daylight time, not abolishing the system.

Our side has shown that daylight saving time damages sleep, public health, and daily routines. The spring clock change raises heart attacks and injuries, and the claimed energy savings are outdated in a modern economy. Parents and students face dark mornings, and workers lose precious rest. Twice-yearly disruptions confuse transport, technology, and international meetings. Stability matters more than tinkering with clocks. Ending daylight saving time would give families predictable schedules, protect vulnerable sleepers, and remove a costly ritual that no longer delivers its promised benefits.

The pro side repeats health worries but never answers the core point: abolishing daylight saving time usually means permanent standard time, with dark evenings and their costs. The evidence shows longer evenings cut crime and help the economy; the pro side has offered no response. Their injury studies measure a brief transition, not a reason to lose evening light all year. If sleep is the concern, we can fix the transition with smoother schedules or adopt permanent daylight time. Abolishing the system is a blunt tool that throws away proven benefits.

Daylight saving time is an outdated practice that disrupts sleep, endangers health, and confuses modern life. The spring transition brings more heart problems and accidents, while families face dark mornings and tired children. Energy savings have vanished with efficient technology, yet businesses still spend money adjusting systems twice a year. Stable, consistent time supports farmers, students, shift workers, and travelers. Abolishing daylight saving time would end unnecessary disruption, protect public health, and give everyone a simpler, safer schedule. We should keep clocks steady and let natural light guide our days.

The pro side keeps repeating sleep and health claims but never answers the central problem: abolishing daylight saving time means dark winter evenings, with higher crime and lower economic activity. Evidence from the U.S. extension shows real electricity savings, and research shows robbery falls when evenings are lighter. If transitions worry them, the answer is permanent daylight time or smoother changes, not abolition. Ending the system would hurt commuters, children, and small businesses while discarding proven benefits. The motion is too blunt; reject it and keep a flexible, evidence-based clock policy.

motion: Single-use coffee cups should carry a tax.

transcript.motion: Single-use coffee cups should carry a tax.

turns.text: Single-use coffee cups are a quiet everyday problem, and a modest tax is the fairest way to change habits. People reach for a disposable cup out of convenience, not malice, so a small price signal nudges them toward reusables without banning anything. Cafés benefit too, because cleaner bins and less litter mean nicer streets and lower cleanup burdens. A tax also signals that convenience is not the same as responsibility, and it rewards businesses that support sustainable choices. Over time, behaviour shifts, culture changes, and the morning coffee ritual becomes less wasteful, all through one simple, transparent policy.

A cup tax sounds tidy, but evidence warns against it. When the UK tried a five-pence charge on single-use bags, usage fell, yet total thin plastic use barely changed because shoppers reused bags as bin liners. Coffee cups are different: they are lined with polyethylene, and a 2023 UK Parliament report found less than three in every thousand are recycled. A tax punishes commuters in areas without washing facilities or reusable-cup schemes. Wales’ 2023 consultation noted concerns about low-income households spending more. Better policy targets industrial recycling infrastructure, not a levy that shifts costs to consumers while producers keep selling the same cups.

My opponent worries about fairness and effectiveness, but the core principle remains simple: when something costs a little more, people think before they act. That is how sensible policy works, and it applies neatly to coffee cups. If reusable options feel inconvenient today, the revenue from the tax can improve them, funding better facilities and incentives. Claims that consumers are unfairly burdened miss the point; we already pay for waste collection and cleanup in hidden ways. A visible, small charge simply makes the true cost clearer, encouraging better choices without coercion.

The pro side says a tax makes costs visible, but visibility does not equal effectiveness. In Ireland, the plastic bag tax was introduced in 2002, yet a 2019 EPA report still found around 15,000 tonnes of plastic bag waste generated annually. A cup tax risks the same plateau: people pay, habits stall, and litter persists. Meanwhile, the claimed revenue is speculative. Cardiff Council estimated street-cleaning costs, but no UK cup levy has shown funds flowing back into reuse infrastructure. The pro side offers no mechanism, only confidence. A tax without recycling access is a surcharge, not a solution.

In closing, the choice is between accepting needless waste or gently steering behaviour toward something better. A small tax does not punish anyone; it simply asks people to notice what they use. It encourages cafés to offer alternatives, helps normalise reusables, and turns a daily habit into a shared responsibility. Even if the change begins modestly, the direction matters. Over years, the routine of grabbing a disposable cup can feel outdated, replaced by a cleaner, more thoughtful practice. That cultural shift, supported by a clear and simple price signal, is worth supporting.

The pro side has offered hope but no evidence. We know from the 2023 House of Commons Environmental Audit Committee evidence that cup recycling remains below one percent, and a tax does not fix that. We also know from Wales’ impact assessment that low-income groups spend proportionally more on takeaway food and drink. A cup tax would charge them for a system they did not design. Better policy would mandate reusable-cup washing stations, standardise compostable linings, and fund collection, not impose a levy that sounds green while leaving the same cups on the same shelves.

motion: Esports should be in the Olympics.

transcript.motion: Esports should be in the Olympics.

turns.text: Esports already meet the IOC’s own test for a sport: competition, strategy, training, and global audiences. The 2022 Asian Games included medal esports events, and the 2023 Asian Games esports title roster drew tens of thousands of in‑person spectators and millions online. Studies from Newzoo and Nielsen show esports viewership rivals many Olympic sports, especially among 18–34 year olds, the audience the Olympics most need. Including titles like Rocket League or chess‑adjacent strategy games would modernize the Games without replacing tradition. Governance exists too: the Global Esports Federation publishes rules and integrity standards, so a pathway to the Olympics is practical, not symbolic.

The Olympics celebrate the apex of human physical mastery, and esports simply are not in that lineage. From the ancient stadion to the modern 100 meters, the Games have honored bodies trained to their limits; we should not abandon that tradition because screens are convenient. If we accept esports because they demand reflexes, then the line between sport and simulation dissolves, and soon the Olympics could become a convention for any popular pastime. The safer course is to keep esports in their own thriving events, like the Asian Games, while reserving the Olympics for physical disciplines whose history and purpose are clear.

Con leans on tradition, but the Olympics have always adapted: archery, shooting, and now breaking are included despite changing physical ideals. Skill is skill, whether in a shooting range or a digital arena. The claim that accepting esports inevitably turns the Games into any pastime is a slippery slope; the IOC already filters sports by governance, universality, and youth relevance. Esports pass those filters. And the Asian Games inclusion Con cites actually supports us: it shows esports can coexist with physical sport without dissolving standards, while giving the Olympics a tested model for staging, anti‑doping, and integrity.

Pro points to new sports like breaking, but that still rests on bodily mastery; comparing it to thumb speed on a controller confuses categories. Tradition is not mere nostalgia: it preserves the Olympic identity that audiences and athletes recognize. The worry about a slippery slope is not fallacious if the criterion becomes any competitive activity with viewers, which would invite poker, trivia, or viral stunts. The Asian Games example cuts both ways: esports are fine there, but the Olympics are different. Keeping them separate protects the Games’ coherence, and avoids forcing the IOC to arbitrate which digital titles deserve medals.

The core question is relevance. Youth engagement with the Olympics is falling; a 2021 IOC survey flagged younger audiences as a strategic risk, and esports are where those audiences already gather. We are not asking the IOC to abandon physical sport, only to add a parallel arena, as it did with shooting and breaking after debate. Con’s fear that any popular pastime could qualify ignores existing filters: governance, universality, and athlete welfare. Esports meet them. Inclusion would modernize the Games, protect their future audience, and honor the Olympic spirit: testing excellence wherever humans compete at the highest level.

Pro confuses popularity with Olympic suitability. Yes, young people watch esports, but the Games are not a ratings exercise; they are a celebration of physical human limits, a tradition that gives the event meaning. If we redefine sport to fit audience trends, we lose the very identity that makes the Olympics worth protecting. The proper response to falling interest is better storytelling for existing sports, not diluting the brand. Esports already flourish in the Asian Games and their own world championships. Keep those vibrant, but keep the Olympics Olympic: a festival of bodily mastery, not a marketplace of screens.
